hints: Recall the shape adopted by 4-coordinate Pt(II) complexes and the bond angle between adjacent positions.
Think how two identical $\text{Cl}$ ligands can be arranged around the central Pt, either next to each other at 90 degrees or opposite each other at 180 degrees.
walkthrough:
Fix the geometry first**
Picture $\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$. Pt is in oxidation state +2, so this is a $d^8$ 4-coordinate complex. For Pt(II) that almost always means square planar, with all four ligands and the metal in one plane and 90 degree angles between neighbours.

Build the cis arrangement**
Put Pt in the centre. Place the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands on adjacent corners of the square, so the $\text{Cl-Pt-Cl}$ angle is 90 degrees. The two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands then occupy the other two adjacent corners. This is the cis isomer, with like ligands side by side. Use wedges or 3D perspective to show the plane.

Build the trans arrangement**
Now swap one pair. Place the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands on opposite corners, so the $\text{Cl-Pt-Cl}$ angle is 180 degrees. The two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands are then also opposite each other. This is the trans isomer, with like ligands across the metal from each other.

Final answer: Isomer 1 (cis): square planar Pt with the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands at 90 degrees to each other (adjacent) and the two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands at 90 degrees to each other.
Isomer 2 (trans): square planar Pt with the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands at 180 degrees to each other (opposite) and the two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands opposite each other.

hints: Compare electronegativities to decide the direction of the $\text{Pt-Cl}$ and $\text{Pt-N}$ bond dipoles, remembering $\text{Cl}$ is strongly electron withdrawing.
walkthrough:
See where the electron density sits**
Think of each bond as a little arrow. $\text{Cl}$ is much more electronegative than Pt, so each $\text{Pt-Cl}$ bond has a strong dipole with $\delta-$ on $\text{Cl}$. In the cis isomer both $\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$ ends lie on the same side of the molecule, so their dipoles add to give a net molecular dipole. In the trans isomer they point in exactly opposite directions, so they cancel and the molecule has no net dipole.

Final answer: The cis isomer is polar (more polar) and the trans isomer is non-polar. In cis, the $\text{Pt-Cl}$ bond dipoles are on the same side and do not cancel, giving an overall dipole. In trans, the identical bond dipoles are opposite and cancel due to symmetry.

hints: Look carefully at the oxaloplatin diagram and identify how many donor atoms each ligand provides and what size ring is formed with Pt.
walkthrough:
Spot that both ligands bite twice**
Look at the structure. On the left, the cyclohexane diamine bonds through two N atoms. On the right, the oxalate bonds through two O atoms. So this is not $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ with four separate ligands, it is $\text{M(AA)(BB)}$ with two chelating bidentate ligands.
Each ligand plus Pt makes a 5-membered ring. That ring is quite small and rigid. It can comfortably bridge two neighbouring sites at 90 degrees, but it simply cannot stretch all the way across the metal to occupy opposite sites at 180 degrees. Therefore only the cis geometry is possible and no trans isomer can form.

Final answer: Oxaloplatin contains two bidentate ligands, the diamine and the oxalate $(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-})$. Each forms a 5-membered chelate ring which can only span adjacent (cis) positions, it is too short to span opposite (trans) positions 180 degrees apart, so only the cis arrangement exists.

hints: Recall how many cis-trans isomers a square planar complex of type $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ should show, and compare with the observation of only one form.
walkthrough:
Use isomer count as a geometry test**
You already saw that square planar $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ gives two isomers, cis and trans. If $[\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{Cl}_2]$ were square planar you would expect to find two different structures. Only one is known, so the premise fails. The alternative 4-coordinate geometry is tetrahedral, in which all positions are equivalent and swapping ligands gives the same arrangement, so only one form exists.

Final answer: The complex cannot be square planar, it must be tetrahedral. A square planar $[\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2\text{Cl}_2]$ would show cis and trans isomers, so observation of only one form indicates tetrahedral stereochemistry where cis-trans isomerism does not occur.

hints: Visualise Ni at the centre of a tetrahedron with bond angles of about 109.5 degrees, using solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds to show 3D depth.
walkthrough:
Draw a true tetrahedron**
Place Ni in the centre. Draw two bonds in the plane, one to $\text{Cl}$ and one to $\text{PR}_3$, then draw one solid wedged bond coming out toward you and one hashed wedged bond going away from you for the other $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{PR}_3$. Label all four ligands clearly as $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$. The key point is that it must look 3D and non-planar, with approximately 109.5 degree angles, quite different from the flat square you drew for Pt.

Final answer: Tetrahedral Ni centre with two $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ ligands and two $\text{Cl}$ ligands arranged tetrahedrally, bond angle about 109.5 degrees, drawn with wedge and hashed bonds to show 3D shape.
